For the rest it is a CLDR estimate (likely subtags): the script in which the language is written, if it is written at all – many of these languages are written only to a limited extent. Brahmic scripts descend from the Indian Brahmi script (Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Thai, Burmese, Tibetan and others); kana and bopomofo developed from Chinese characters. oDatech.nadpis: About the data and how the atlas was made
oDatech.uvod: The atlas is built on open databases put together by linguists from all over the world. Here is where everything comes from, what is certain and what is only an estimate.

p: Each dot is one language. The list of languages comes from Glottolog, an open database of the world's languages run by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The atlas takes everything Glottolog lists as a language and gives a location: {g} languages.
A dot stands where Glottolog places the language, usually in the middle of the area where it is spoken. Even a language spoken all over the world has just one dot, at its home.

Left out are only Glottolog's special bins: bookkeeping entries, languages known only by name and languages we know so little about that they cannot be classified. Esperanto, Interlingua and Interslavic have no dot because they did not arise in any one place; they are still in the list and in search.

There is no sharp line between a language and a dialect, and history and politics often play a part. The atlas follows Glottolog's decisions. That is why Bavarian has a dot but Australian English does not – Glottolog counts it as a variety of English. Dialects are listed on the language card, and searching for one finds its language.

Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin are very easy to understand for each other's speakers and rest on the same dialect base, Shtokavian. Linguistically they are close standard varieties of one shared language; officially and socially they are separate languages today. Glottolog lists them as one language, Serbo-Croatian, which has a dot on the globe. The atlas also has Serbian and Croatian as separate languages with a greeting, but they have no dot of their own. Hmong, on the other hand, is several languages in Glottolog and one entry in the atlas. That is why the list has {n} entries and the globe {g} dots.

For 163 selected languages the atlas gives a greeting, an approximate pronunciation, a note, the number of speakers and the area of distribution. These are compiled by hand and the notes are fact-checked.
The pronunciation guide is only approximate. Speaker numbers are rounded estimates that include second-language speakers.
The orange area on the globe is drawn by hand and approximate, not measured. There are no open data with exact language boundaries for the whole world.
The Play pronunciation button uses the device's speech synthesis; for some languages the device has no voice.
The illustrations show the typical landscape and vernacular architecture of the region the language comes from. They do not depict particular places.
Vitality: the UNESCO scale (safe to extinct) based on Glottolog data.

Typology (word order, cases, tone, consonant inventory… – 24 features): WALS Online, the World Atlas of Language Structures (Dryer & Haspelmath 2013). WALS describes a sample of about 2,600 languages; the others have no value. For the map some values are merged into groups; the language card always shows the exact WALS value.
Number of sounds: PHOIBLE. Sample text: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR in Unicode).
Speaker numbers: Wikidata; where missing, an estimate from Unicode CLDR.

Script and official status: Unicode CLDR (languageData, territoryInfo). Official status is national, de facto or regional; CLDR records it only for languages whose country data it tracks, so it is often missing for minority languages even where they have some official standing. For other languages the script map (Maps › Script) uses the script estimate from CLDR likelySubtags, so that the map shows a script for about 6,800 languages in all. The language card marks an estimate as such.
Relatives and the family tree: the Glottolog tree, with Glottolog's branch names.
Nothing is made up: if a source has no data, the card does not show it.

oddily.h: Languages of antiquity and Language stories
p: The Atlas writes the pages on ancient civilizations and the Language stories from the scholarly literature listed at the end of each page, and checks the facts before publication. The photographs come from Wikimedia Commons and have free licences (CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC0 or public domain); the author and licence are given with each image. Cuneiform signs and Anatolian hieroglyphs are rendered with the Noto fonts (SIL Open Font License).
Country borders and land come from Natural Earth (simplified, scale 1:110 million). Relief and the sea floor come from Natural Earth and NOAA ETOPO1.

navod.napoveda: Full guide – all features of the atlas
navod.uvod: The atlas shows all 7,967 languages of the world after Glottolog on an interactive globe. This guide describes every feature and how to use it with a mouse, touch or the keyboard.

p: Rotate: drag with the mouse or one finger. Zoom: mouse wheel, pinch with two fingers, the + and − buttons at the top right of the globe, or the + and − keys.

Each dot is one language, placed where Glottolog locates it, usually in the middle of the area where it is spoken. Click a dot to open the language card. The selected language and its relatives are named next to their dots; names of all languages from 2× zoom can be switched on in Settings (Names).
Clicking a country away from the dots highlights the country and all its languages and shows their number according to Glottolog.
The Whole world button and the Language Atlas logo in the top left return the globe to its initial view.

163 selected languages have a detailed card: an illustration of the region, a greeting with approximate pronunciation and a Play pronunciation button (it uses the device's speech synthesis). Below are the number of speakers, the language family and vitality, and the tabs Note (note, distribution, official status, script, dialects), Vitality, Structure and Relatives.

All other languages have the tabs Overview (vitality, distribution, official status, script, dialects, speaker numbers, sample text), Structure (WALS typology, PHOIBLE sound inventory, documentation) and Relatives.

Official status lists the countries where the language is official – nationally, de facto (without explicit legal status) or regionally (in part of the country only). Script lists the scripts the language is usually written in, the most common first. Both come from Unicode CLDR and are available for about 800 languages.
The Structure tab gives the exact value for each WALS feature; click a feature name to open its typology map.
Arcs on the globe lead from the selected language to its closest relatives. The language family tree line shows its classification in the Glottolog tree.
The chain button copies a link to the language. On a phone the card sits at the bottom of the screen: drag it up to enlarge it, down to shrink or close it.
You can search for a language, a country or a dialect. The cross in the search box clears it.
Sort by language family, alphabetically or by continent. Languages with a detailed card are shown as large tiles, the others below them.

The Language of the Day changes at midnight and always states why it was chosen: either a day associated with that language (see the Calendar of language days) or the journey around the world to the next nearest language. On the European Day of Languages (26 September) all European languages of the atlas are shown instead.

The round buttons below the globe (in two rows on a phone) open the main parts of the atlas: Ancient languages, Language stories, Family tree, Maps, Vitality and Settings. Random language sits in the header of the language list, next to the language count, and opens the card of a randomly selected language.

Family tree shows the fan-shaped tree of a language family: with a language selected, its family, otherwise the family chosen in the menu at the top. Drag to move, use the wheel or two fingers to zoom, click a branch to focus on it and click a language to select it. The Circular overview button offers another view of all families at once: the width of a segment is the number of languages; click a segment or a row of the list to go deeper, and click the centre of the circle to go back up. Families with fewer than 25 languages are under Smaller families; isolates, sign and artificial languages and pidgins under Outside families. Back to the tree or Open the family tree returns to the fan.

Vitality opens a page on language endangerment: the number of languages in each degree of the UNESCO scale, the breakdown by world region and by the fifteen largest language families (with a link to the family tree), endangered languages in the atlas, awakening languages, and the method with sources. From there you can colour the globe and the family tree by vitality – the tree then shows which branches of a family are endangered or extinct – and tick which degrees stay visible (a filter). While the colours are on, a key sits below the globe; click it to open the page again. The page also opens from a link on the language card and from the address #vitality.
Maps opens an overview of all colour maps with previews: script, vitality and 24 typological features from WALS. Choosing a map closes the window and colours the globe.
Settings: automatic rotation, language names and sign languages (all, none or only these).
Zoom in and out (+ and −) and the Whole world button sit discreetly at the top right of the globe, below the help question mark; on a phone, pinch with two fingers to zoom.

In the Maps window you can choose one of 24 features in five areas (phonology, morphology, word order, clause structure, lexicon). The languages take the colour of their value and a key appears at the bottom right with the number of languages, a description of the feature and a link to the relevant WALS chapter.

After a choice the window closes; Another map… in the key or the Maps medallion opens it again. Clicking a value in the key highlights only the languages with that value. WALS describes a sample of about 2,600 languages; the other dots stay grey.

The Script map (in the Maps window) colours languages by their main script: Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Brahmic scripts (India, Southeast Asia, Tibet), Chinese characters with kana and bopomofo, and other scripts. The legend at the bottom right gives the number of languages; tapping a group highlights it alone.

The data come from Unicode CLDR. For languages about which CLDR keeps detailed data the script is attested; for the rest it is a CLDR estimate (the script in which the language is written, if it is written at all), and the language card marks it as such. The script map and a typological map are not shown at the same time.

On a language card choose Compare with another language and select the second language on the globe, in the list or by searching. The comparison shows the relationship and the closest common ancestor, shared and differing WALS features, sound inventories, speaker numbers and script.

The Ancient languages medallion below the globe opens the menu of civilizations; the search also finds them, for example “egypt”. Each item opens a civilization page focused on language and script: history, sample signs, the story of decipherment, related words, grammar, a timeline, photographs and literature. Two overviews come first in the menu: the family tree of scripts (where each alphabet came from, with a table of the word “king” in twenty scripts) and a glossary of terms (abjad, abugida, determinative, boustrophedon…). Pages on Sumer and Akkad, Ancient Egypt, Elam and Urartu, Ancient India, the Hittites, Ancient China, the Phoenicians, the Hebrews and Arameans, Ancient Greece, the Celts, the Etruscans, Ancient Persia, Ancient Rome, the Armenians and Georgians, the Germanic peoples and runes, Aksum, Korea and Hangul, the Göktürks and the Orkhon script, Japan and kana, the Slavs and Great Moravia, the Maya, the Aztecs and the Incas are ready so far.

The page opens above the globe; close it with the cross, the Escape key or by tapping outside it. The “‹ Languages of antiquity” button at the top left returns to the list of civilizations, and the end of each page links to the others. The buttons in the section on languages on the globe show the extinct languages concerned on the globe. The page can also be opened from the language card (for example of Egyptian, Coptic, Hittite or Luwian) and with the links thelanguageatlas.com/#egypt and #hittites; on the website it is also a separate page.

The Language stories medallion below the globe opens the menu of stories: thematic pages in the same style as Languages of antiquity, grouped into Travelling words, Languages through time, People and languages, and Mysteries. Ready so far: Tea and other travelling words (why the world says either “cha” or “tea”), Czech words in other languages (robot, dollar, howitzer, pistol, polka – what is attested and what is disputed), From Latin to the Romance languages, How Standard Czech came about (from Old Czech glosses through the Bible of Kralice and the National Revival to the spelling rules and Standard versus Common Czech), Languages coming back (Welsh, Māori, Manx, Hebrew) and Linguistic mysteries (undeciphered scripts, language isolates and disputed families).

The Show on the globe button on the tea page closes the page and colours the globe with the WALS map of the origin of the word for tea. The search finds the stories too (for example “robot”); links look like thelanguageatlas.com/#tea, and on the website each story is also a separate page under /stories/.

The pages about tea and about Czech words have a section Word journeys on the globe with buttons for tea, coffee, sugar, orange, chocolate, tomato, check and mate, alcohol, zero and cipher, shampoo, robot and dollar. The globe flies over the area the word travelled through and arcs are drawn step by step from the source language; the word form and the language appear at each dot. A dashed arc marks a disputed route. The panel at the top right (below the globe on a phone) lists the steps with dates and notes; tapping a step opens the language card. Play again repeats the animation and the other buttons switch to another word. Close it with the cross, the Escape key or the Whole world button; links look like #cesta-caj.

oddily.h: Keyboard The Czech card has a Journey of Czech button in the Interesting fact tab: on the globe, streams spread stage by stage from Proto-Indo-European through the Slavic migrations to Czech, with a timeline, playback and a text for each stage.
p: Tab moves between controls. One Tab enters the language list; the arrow keys move between tiles, Home and End jump to the start and end, and Enter selects a language.
The + and − keys zoom the globe. Escape closes a window, the card or a panel.

oddily.h: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar
p: At the end of the language list (on a phone, at the end of the page) there is a folded line: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar. Click it to expand it.

Calendar of language days: the days of the year associated with a particular language (language days, public holidays, anniversaries). It opens at the nearest day; click a language to show it on the globe.
About the data: the sources (Glottolog, WALS, PHOIBLE, Wikidata, Unicode CLDR and others), their versions and licences, and why the list has more entries than there are dots on the globe.
Full guide: this text.
Languages with a detailed card (website only): all 163 languages on one page. Each opens as a card; use the arrows to move to the next one.
Contact: comments and corrections to info@atlasjazyku.cz. Below are the data sources and their licences.
In the top right you can switch the interface language (Česky) and the light or dark theme. Your choices are saved.
Search also knows languages constructed for literature and film (such as Quenya or Klingon); they are shown separately from natural languages.

vitStranka.podtitul: How endangered the world’s languages are · the UNESCO scale
vitStranka.uvod: Vitality describes whether a language is being passed on to the next generation. The atlas uses UNESCO’s six-degree scale, from safe to extinct, and separately marks awakening languages – languages that Glottolog lists as extinct but that people are learning and using again. The data come from Glottolog and cover all {n} languages on the globe.
vitStranka.souhrn: {n} languages, or {p} of all languages on the globe, are endangered to some degree.
vitStranka.barvyZap: Colour the globe and family tree by vitality
vitStranka.stupneUvod: The length of each bar gives the number of languages. Ticked degrees stay visible on the globe, in the family tree, in the list and in search; untick a degree to hide its languages (the filter works without the colours too).
vitStranka.filtrTitulek: Show or hide the languages of this degree
vitStranka.bezUdajePopis: Glottolog gives no degree of endangerment for the language.
vitStranka.oblastiUvod: The regions are Glottolog’s macroareas. The bar shows the share of the region’s languages at each degree (colours as above).
vitStranka.rodinyUvod: The fifteen largest language families in Glottolog (excluding isolates, sign languages and groupings that are not families). The button opens the family tree; with vitality colours on, its languages are coloured by degree, so you can see which branches are endangered or extinct.
vitStranka.atlasUvod: Languages with a detailed card that Glottolog lists as endangered to some degree or as awakening, most endangered first. Click to open the language card.
vitStranka.probouzeneUvod: There are {n} awakening languages. Glottolog classifies them as extinct, but people are learning and using them again. Glottolog does not treat this as a separate degree; the atlas recognises them from the note “Awakening” (Catalogue of Endangered Languages) or “Reawakening” (Ethnologue) that Glottolog carries over from the original source. Click a language to show it on the globe.
metodika: The degrees follow the intergenerational transmission criterion in the UNESCO expert group document Language Vitality and Endangerment (2003). Their names and descriptions follow the Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger (Moseley 2010), which adopted the scale and renamed two degrees (unsafe to vulnerable, definitively to definitely endangered).

Glottolog gives most languages an Agglomerated Endangerment Status (AES), compiled mainly from UNESCO, Ethnologue and the Catalogue of Endangered Languages (ElCat). Each of its degrees corresponds to exactly one UNESCO degree: not endangered = safe, threatened = vulnerable, shifting = definitely endangered, moribund = severely endangered, nearly extinct = critically endangered, extinct = extinct.

The assessments date from different years and the sources sometimes disagree, so the degree is an indication rather than a precise measurement. The extinct languages include languages known only from historical records, such as Hittite and Sumerian, as well as Latin, which has no native speakers although it is still used as a second language (for example by the Holy See). {n} languages have no data. The Glottolog data were downloaded on {d}.
zdroje: UNESCO Ad Hoc Expert Group on Endangered Languages (2003): Language Vitality and Endangerment. Paris: UNESCO.
Moseley, Christopher (ed.) (2010): Atlas of the World’s Languages in Danger. 3rd edn. Paris: UNESCO Publishing.

velryby.prepis: the “1+1+3” coda of the sperm whales off Dominica
velryby.prehrajPozn: A sketch of the rhythm made of clicks generated in the browser, not a recording.

p: The sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus) communicates with codas – short series of roughly 3 to 40 clicks in a fixed rhythm. They were first described by William Watkins and William Schevill in 1977.

Females and their young live in stable family units. Units with a similar repertoire of codas form a so-called vocal clan; clans differ much like dialects, and calves most likely learn the repertoire from those around them. Off the island of Dominica in the Caribbean, the typical coda of clan EC1 is “1+1+3”: two spaced clicks followed by three quick ones.

In 2024 the Project CETI team (Sharma et al., Nature Communications) showed on recordings from Dominica that codas also differ in finer features: tempo, rhythm, gradual lengthening and shortening of successive codas (rubato) and an extra click (ornamentation). These features combine independently, so there are far more distinct codas than was thought.
The authors speak of a “sperm whale phonetic alphabet”. What the individual combinations mean, nobody knows yet.

Male humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) sing songs lasting from a few minutes to tens of minutes, repeated for hours. They are structured on several levels: individual sounds form phrases, repeated phrases form themes, and themes form the song. They were described by Roger Payne and Scott McVay in 1971.

The males of one population sing essentially the same song at a given time, and the song gradually changes. In the South Pacific, new songs spread from eastern Australia eastwards from population to population (Garland et al. 2011), much like a cultural fashion.

A 2025 study (Arnon et al., Science) split the songs into recurring segments with a method inspired by how infants find words in speech: it placed boundaries where the probability of one sound following another drops. The frequency of the segments follows Zipf’s law, like words in human languages. In experiments with humans such a distribution makes learning easier; it does not mean that the segments carry meaning.
Humpback song is also on the 1977 Voyager Golden Record: it follows the greetings in 55 human languages, as a backdrop to greetings from UN delegates.

A bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) has its own so-called signature whistle, which differs from the whistles of others (Caldwell and Caldwell 1965). It develops in the first months of life and often stays with the animal for life (Janik and Sayigh 2013).

Dolphins occasionally copy another dolphin's signature whistle, mostly that of a close companion they have been separated from (King et al. 2013). Dolphins respond to a playback copy of their own whistle, but not to the whistles of others (King and Janik 2013). It thus works much like a name.
Dolphins remember the whistles of former companions even after more than twenty years apart (Bruck 2013).

In the 1980s Louis Herman in Hawaii taught two female bottlenose dolphins artificial languages: Akeakamai a language of gestures and Phoenix one of computer-generated sounds. They understood new sentences too and distinguished word order: taking the surfboard to the hoop is different from taking the hoop to the surfboard (Herman et al. 1984). But this was understanding of a language invented by humans, not the dolphins' own speech.

Denise Herzing's Wild Dolphin Project has been recording Atlantic spotted dolphins (Stenella frontalis) in the Bahamas since 1985. In 2025 Google, together with the project and Georgia Tech, presented an AI model called DolphinGemma, which learns the structure of dolphin sounds and is meant to help find recurring patterns in the recordings. No peer-reviewed results have been published yet (as of September 2026).

The orca or killer whale (Orcinus orca) is the largest of the dolphins. Fish-eating orcas off British Columbia and Washington State live in family groups descended from one mother (matrilines), and each group has its own set of stereotyped calls. Groups that share some of their calls form an acoustic clan (Ford 1991). Calves probably learn the calls from their mothers, and the group keeps them with little change for decades, which is why they are spoken of as dialects.

Orcas that hunt marine mammals such as seals, sea lions and porpoises (Bigg's orcas) call much less than fish-eaters, probably because their prey would hear them. They call mainly after a successful kill and during play at the surface (Deecke et al. 2005).

Orcas can imitate unfamiliar sounds. Orcas kept together with bottlenose dolphins began producing more whistles and clicks, as dolphins do, and one picked up a chirp sequence that humans had taught the dolphins (Musser et al. 2014). A captive female, Wikie, imitated human words such as “hello” and “bye bye” (Abramson et al. 2018). That does not mean she understood them.

At least not in the sense in which English or British Sign Language is a language. Human language combines units that mean something, according to rules, into ever new utterances. We know that cetacean communication has a complex structure, is passed on by learning and differs between groups much like dialects. Sperm whale codas and orca calls are known to reveal which group the caller belongs to, and dolphin signature whistles work much like names. But we do not know whether codas, humpback songs or orca calls carry word-like meaning, let alone whether they combine into new utterances.
That is why cetaceans have no dot on the globe: the atlas records human languages according to Glottolog.

p: According to chapter eleven of the Book of Genesis, all people spoke one language. In the land of Shinar they built a city and a tower whose top was to reach the heavens, to “make a name” for themselves. The Lord confused their language so that they would not understand one another, and scattered them over all the earth.

The text explains the city’s name by a pun: it links Hebrew Bavel with the verb bālal, “to confuse”. The real origin of the name is different. The Babylonians interpreted it as Bāb-ili, “gate of god”, and the name may be even older.

The tower was most likely modelled on the ziggurat Etemenanki, Sumerian for “house of the foundation of heaven and earth”, beside Marduk’s temple Esagila in Babylon. According to his own inscriptions, its restoration was completed by Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605–562 BCE), at the time when part of the people of Judah lived in Babylon in exile.

The so-called Esagila tablet, a cuneiform copy of an older text made at Uruk in 229 BCE (in the Seleucid period), gives a square base about 91 metres on each side. Only the foundations of the tower remain today.
Among the {n} languages of the atlas there are {r} language families and {i} isolates whose relationship to other languages has not been demonstrated.

Whether all languages go back to one common ancestor cannot be proven. The comparative method, by which linguists reconstruct proto-languages, reaches back, by common estimates, no more than roughly 6,000 to 10,000 years, but people have been speaking far longer. Linguistic diversity did not arise all at once: languages change with every generation, and groups that stop talking to each other stop understanding each other within centuries.
